Logging to local or network paths detected
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\log4Net.xml

Explanation

Logging to local or network paths detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, prefer Application Insights/App Service logging. If filesystem logs are required, write to a mounted Azure Files share configured via storage mounts and Key Vault secrets.

Logging APIs that write to disk might not work on Azure App Service or Container.

Use logging that stores logs in locations outside of the host unless its specifically required by your app. You can also use logging capabilities embedded in Azure, such as Azure App Service logging or Application Insights.

For migrating to AKS, use LogMonitor tool that can capture logs written to files, the console, or write logs and redirect them to Azure.

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Global.asax.csLine 42

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Web.config

Explanation

Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move session to Azure Cache for Redis or Cosmos DB. In-proc session impedes scale-out; Managed Instance does not change session semantics.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

In-proc or local process stored session state not immediately prevents an application from working in Azure, however, is not recommended because it would make scaling the Azure App Service or Azure Kubernetes Service more difficult.

Azure provides multiple ways to store session state in a scalable way using Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Cosmos DB or other services.

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
eShopLegacy.Utilities\eShopLegacy.Utilities.csproj
eShopPorted\eShopPorted.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.

Deprecated Remoting & Serialization
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy .NET Remoting, BinaryFormatter, and related serialization APIs that are deprecated and removed for security reasons. Remoting provided distributed object communication but had significant security vulnerabilities. Migrate to gRPC, HTTP APIs, or modern serialization (System.Text.Json, protobuf).
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
ASP.NET Framework (System.Web)
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy ASP.NET Framework APIs for web applications (System.Web.*) that don't exist in ASP.NET Core due to architectural differences. ASP.NET Core represents a complete redesign of the web framework. Migrate to ASP.NET Core equivalents or consider System.Web.Adapters package for compatibility.

Architecture Diagram

The solution contains two catalog web applications and a shared serialization utility. The legacy MVC application and its ASP.NET Core port are separate deployables with their own persistence configuration.

Application Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Client["Client Layer"] Browser["Web Browser"] ApiClient["HTTP API Client"] end subgraph Legacy["Legacy Application - ASP.NET MVC 5"] LegacyMvc["MVC Views and Web API"] LegacyServices["Catalog Services"] LegacyOrm["Entity Framework 6"] end subgraph Ported["Ported Application - ASP.NET Core MVC"] PortedMvc["MVC Views and API Controllers"] PortedServices["Catalog Services"] PortedOrm["Entity Framework Core"] end subgraph Data["Data Stores"] LegacyDb[("SQL Server LocalDB - legacy catalog")] PortedDb[("SQL Server LocalDB - ported catalog")] Images[("Local product image files")] end subgraph CrossCutting["Cross-Cutting"] Telemetry["Application Insights and log4net"] Serialization["Shared Binary Serialization Utility"] end Browser -->|"HTTP requests"| LegacyMvc Browser -->|"HTTP requests"| PortedMvc ApiClient -->|"HTTP API requests"| LegacyMvc ApiClient -->|"HTTP API requests"| PortedMvc LegacyMvc -->|"catalog operations"| LegacyServices PortedMvc -->|"catalog operations"| PortedServices LegacyServices -->|"queries and updates"| LegacyOrm PortedServices -->|"queries and updates"| PortedOrm LegacyOrm -->|"EF6 persistence"| LegacyDb PortedOrm -->|"EF Core persistence"| PortedDb LegacyMvc -->|"serves catalog pictures"| Images PortedMvc -->|"serves catalog pictures"| Images LegacyMvc -->|"binary brand response"| Serialization PortedMvc -->|"binary brand response"| Serialization LegacyMvc -.->|"telemetry and logging"| Telemetry PortedMvc -.->|"logging"| Telemetry

Data Storage & External Services

Both applications are configured for SQL Server LocalDB with integrated Windows authentication, but use separate database names and persistence frameworks. Catalog pictures are read from local image files. No message broker, cache, external business API, or service-discovery component was identified; Application Insights and log4net provide telemetry/logging integration.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The ported application is a parallel implementation rather than a downstream service; there is no cross-application API or shared database access path.
  • ICatalogService isolates MVC and API controllers from either EF-backed catalog operations or the optional mock implementation.
  • Autofac provides module-based dependency registration; UseMockData selects the in-memory service mode.

DTOs & Contracts

CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, and CatalogType are domain entities also used in MVC model binding and API responses. PaginatedItemsViewModel is the catalog-list response model. Each Files API projects brands to a BrandDTO (Id, Brand) and serializes the collection to a binary stream; no immutable request/response record types or OpenAPI/protobuf/GraphQL definitions were found. MVC JSON uses framework defaults; no custom JSON serializer settings were identified.

Communication Patterns

Controller-to-service and service-to-EF interactions are synchronous method calls. EF6 and EF Core issue queries and updates to their respective SQL Server LocalDB databases; there is no cross-application HTTP call, message queue, event stream, retry policy, circuit breaker, or service discovery. UseMockData switches a project to an in-memory service. No application authentication or authorization filter/middleware is configured; the IIS Express profile enables anonymous access, and local launch URLs include HTTP and HTTPS without an application-wide TLS enforcement policy.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports maintaining and browsing a product catalog, including product images, brands, types, stock values, and prices. It does not implement shopping carts, checkout, payment processing, or customer accounts.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalog ManagementProduct offered in the catalog, with price, stock, and image referenceBelongs to one CatalogBrand and one CatalogType
CatalogBrandCatalog ManagementProduct brand lookup valueGroups catalog items
CatalogTypeCatalog ManagementProduct type/category lookup valueGroups catalog items

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopLegacyMVCCatalog ManagementCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeIts EF6 LocalDB database and local picture files
eShopPortedCatalog ManagementCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeIts EF Core LocalDB database and local picture files

The applications are parallel implementations. They do not exchange catalog entities or call one another; each owns its own catalog copy.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse the Catalog

  1. A visitor opens the catalog page with optional pageSize and pageIndex.
  2. The CatalogController asks ICatalogService for a page of catalog items.
  3. In database mode, CatalogService queries items with their brand and type. In mock mode, CatalogServiceMock reads the in-memory list and joins the preconfigured lookup values.
  4. The application returns a paginated view model and renders the catalog. Picture URIs link to the picture route.

Workflow 2: Create or Edit a Catalog Item

  1. A catalog operator submits the create or edit form.
  2. MVC model binding constructs a CatalogItem. ModelState.IsValid checks annotations before saving.
  3. Create assigns an identifier through the legacy HiLo sequence generator, ported EF Core identity generation, or the mock implementation's next identifier.
  4. The service persists the catalog item and its brand/type references, then the controller redirects to the catalog page. The edit flow updates the selected item.

Workflow 3: Delete a Catalog Item or View Its Picture

The delete form submits an item ID and removes the corresponding catalog item. A picture request resolves the selected catalog record and reads its configured image file. The brands API's demo DELETE action reports success for an existing brand but intentionally does not delete it.

Cross-Service Data Flows

No cross-service composition or data synchronization flow was identified. Each application queries its own catalog database or mock list. Brand and type records are joined locally by EF navigation properties or by the mock service. Product-image responses are read from local files, not from an external image service.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant Operator participant Controller as "Catalog Controller" participant Service as "Catalog Service" participant Database as "Local Catalog Database" participant Model as "CatalogItem" Operator->>Controller: Submit new catalog item Controller->>Model: Bind submitted fields Controller->>Controller: Validate model annotations alt Model is valid Controller->>Service: Create catalog item Service->>Database: Allocate identifier and save item Database-->>Service: Save completed Service-->>Controller: Create completed Controller-->>Operator: Redirect to catalog page else Model is invalid Controller-->>Operator: Return form with validation errors end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Catalog item names are required. Prices must match the decimal format and fall within the configured range; stock, restock, and maximum-stock values have nonnegative bounded ranges.
  • Catalog items require brand and type relationships in the EF mappings. Their default image filename is dummy.png.
  • The legacy database initializer uses SQL sequence scripts and CSV customization data when enabled; the ported implementation uses EF Core migrations and configured seed rows.
  • Create, edit, and delete operations have no multi-step business state transition. There is no order lifecycle or payment workflow.
  • MVC create/edit/delete POST handlers use anti-forgery validation. No application-level role or resource-ownership policy was identified.
  • Errors flow through the MVC error handling configuration; no domain audit trail or compensating transaction was found.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The ported project targets ASP.NET Core and EF Core 2.2, which are out of support; it also targets .NET Framework 4.6.1. The legacy project targets .NET Framework 4.7.2 and Entity Framework 6.2.0. Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.1 is affected by CVE-2024-21907; the ported project declares 13.0.2.

Notable Observations

  • The solution contains parallel legacy and ported web applications with overlapping functionality and distinct dependency versions.
  • The legacy project declares Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.1 while the ported project declares 13.0.2.
  • The legacy project uses BinaryFormatter through a shared serialization utility.
  • No test-scoped package dependencies or dedicated test project were detected in the solution.

Caching Strategy

No distributed or provider-backed cache, EF second-level cache, cache annotations, or explicit cache TTL was identified. The optional mock service keeps catalog state in an in-memory list; this is application data mode, not a cache.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The two applications implement the same catalog domain but use distinct databases and have no cross-service API or direct database exchange. The legacy and ported services are each the source of truth for their own catalog copy. Catalog items reference their own application's brand and type tables; no CQRS, outbox, or event-driven synchronization mechanism was found.
